A pay rise, extra tax and a benefit phase-out: compare the full before-and-after change

Four charts separate a hypothetical flat earnings tax from a cash-benefit phase-out, then compare local marginal offsets with the amount retained across a complete pay increase.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a hypothetical flat tax from a separate benefit phase-out

Interactive planning lab

Modeled monthly resources after the selected raise$1,760
Increase in monthly resources$110
Extra tax plus lost benefit / selected gross raise45.00%

An invented monthly tax-and-benefit system, not the law, eligibility rules or tax year of any country. All amounts are hypothetical CAD per month. Tax is a flat entered percentage of ALL gross earnings, without brackets, allowances, credits or payroll contributions. A separate nontaxable cash benefit begins at the entered maximum and falls by the selected rate on gross earnings above a fixed CAD 1,500 threshold, stopping at zero. The benefit is never negative; no cliff or repayment debt is modeled. Both earnings and the benefit are assumed received in the same modeled month; no prior-year assessment, withholding/refund settlement or receipt lag is calculated. Resources equal gross earnings minus this modeled tax plus this modeled benefit. The selected-raise offset share is (extra tax + lost benefit) / the full gross increase; it is undefined when the increase is zero. The right-hand local offset at the selected STARTING income is 70.00%, which can differ from the full-increase share when a phase-out boundary is crossed. A zero phase-out rate keeps the benefit constant. Combined local offsets may exceed 100% under deliberately extreme entered assumptions, and negative resource gains are retained. No employee/employer contributions, household costs, inflation, work incentives or behaviour, real benefit entitlement, tax deduction or personal affordability is inferred. This is not an OECD country estimate or an employer-labour-cost tax wedge.

The central idea

Calculate the tax and benefit at both income endpoints. A rate applying to the next dollar may differ from the average offset across a raise that crosses a phase-out boundary.

01

Define the earnings tax and cash benefit separately

A gross pay rise can change more than the tax charged on earnings. If a separate cash benefit falls as income rises, the amount retained can also depend on that benefit's phase-out range.

OECD's discussion of work incentives explains this general interaction between higher taxes and reduced support. The example here illustrates the arithmetic with an invented system. It does not reproduce the rates, household types or rules used for any OECD country.

The model charges a flat 20% tax on all monthly gross earnings. A separate CAD 300 monthly cash benefit remains at its maximum through CAD 1,500 of gross earnings. Above that fixed threshold, it falls by CAD 0.50 per additional dollar until it reaches zero.

The benefit is assumed nontaxable within this fictional system, and both amounts are received in the same modeled month. There are no brackets, allowances, payroll contributions, assessment lags or tax settlements. Monthly resources are defined as gross earnings minus the modeled tax plus the modeled benefit.

02

Reconcile the selected raise using both endpoints

The starting gross income is CAD 2,000 per month. The flat tax is CAD 400. The benefit has fallen from CAD 300 to CAD 50 because CAD 500 of earnings lies above the threshold, creating CAD 250 of phase-out. Starting modeled resources are therefore CAD 1,650.

A CAD 200 monthly gross increase brings earnings to CAD 2,200. Tax rises to CAD 440, while the benefit has reached zero. After-raise modeled resources are CAD 1,760.

The change is CAD 200 gross increase − CAD 40 extra tax − CAD 50 benefit lost = CAD 110. The waterfall presents those three changes as a reconciliation rather than treating the benefit reduction as another income-tax charge.

The lost benefit is capped at what the person was still receiving before the raise. Applying a 50% phase-out to all CAD 200 would incorrectly deduct CAD 100 even though only CAD 50 of benefit remained. A phase-out rate needs its starting balance and endpoint.

03

Distinguish the next-dollar offset from the full-raise offset

At the default starting income of CAD 2,000, the next small increase lies inside the benefit's phase-out range. The right-hand local offset is 20% extra tax plus 50% benefit reduction, or 70%. Within that segment, CAD 1 of extra gross earnings adds CAD 0.30 to modeled resources.

The full CAD 200 raise crosses the point where the benefit is exhausted, at CAD 2,100. The first CAD 100 retains CAD 30. The next CAD 100 has no further benefit to lose and retains CAD 80 after the same flat tax.

Together those pieces retain CAD 110. Extra tax plus lost benefit totals CAD 90, giving a 45% offset over the complete CAD 200 raise. That average over the selected change is different from the 70% local rate at its starting point.

The headline ratio therefore uses the whole chosen increase as its denominator. It is not the average tax burden on all earnings and is not automatically a marginal rate applying to every dollar. With a zero gross increase, the ratio is undefined and is shown as N/A.

04

A resource level and a resource increase answer different questions

The first chart plots modeled resource levels against gross earnings. The gap between its two lines is the current benefit. When that gap closes, the benefit has reached zero; it is not a second tax payment or a new wage deduction.

The curve includes the exact phase-out start and exhaustion point, when the latter falls inside the chart. These are changes in slope. The fictional benefit falls continuously, so the model does not create a sudden eligibility cliff.

The starting-income comparison instead holds the gross raise fixed and recalculates the gain from several starting points. A row above the phase-out range can retain more of the same raise because there is no benefit left to lose.

That larger incremental gain does not mean the higher-income scenario receives a larger benefit. It also does not compare complete household living standards. Read the resource-level chart alongside changes, rather than interpreting one gain bar as a total budget.

05

Retain boundary cases instead of forcing a favorable answer

A zero phase-out rate keeps the benefit constant at its entered maximum. A zero benefit removes the phase-out channel entirely. In either case, a gross increase changes resources only through the fictional flat earnings tax.

The benefit never becomes negative. Once exhausted, it cannot keep reducing resources as earnings rise. At the phase-out start, the displayed right-hand local rate includes the reduction on the next dollar; at exhaustion, it excludes any further reduction.

The controls also permit deliberately extreme combinations. With a 60% flat tax and a 100% benefit-reduction rate inside an active phase-out segment, the combined local offset is 160%. An extra CAD 100 entirely within that segment would reduce modeled resources by CAD 60.

The charts preserve such negative changes. They describe the entered fictional rules, rather than a real country's incentives or advice to reject additional work. The calculation includes no career progression, pension accrual, working costs, noncash services or household preferences.

06

Verify real assessment periods before using a budget number

The matrix varies starting income and the size of the gross increase while retaining the entered tax and benefit assumptions. Every cell recalculates both endpoints. It does not extend one local rate across a boundary without checking whether benefit remains.

A real comparison needs the actual income definitions, applicable household circumstances, assessment period and timing of receipts. A benefit based on an earlier tax year may respond at a different date from payroll income. A withholding change may also differ from final tax.

Those details are absent from this deliberately same-month illustration. Before changing a spending or saving commitment, obtain the applicable rules and confirmed amounts, then place the receipts and obligations on their actual dates. The resource change here is not a bank balance or an affordability finding.

The useful habit is to reconcile the gross increase with each additional tax or lost payment separately. Keep the denominator visible, distinguish the local slope from the full-change ratio and stop benefit reductions at the actual remaining benefit. That makes the effect of a pay change understandable before it enters a household plan.
